items.why: Tests Jeroboam’s failure to reform, contrasting it with his continued appointment of priests.
“Gives the message” does not clearly distinguish its original proclaimer from the father repeating it.
Distinguishes the collective victory over four descendants from Jonathan’s killing of one.
Requires connecting the officer’s warning with his death rather than mistaking the prophet for the victim.
Clearly distinguishes the old prophet who rides from the sons who saddle his donkey.
Tests the meaningful difference between the covenant including the Lord and the separate king–people covenant.
Uses burial as a next-event cue rather than testing Jotham’s meaningful transition from governing to kingship.
Distinguishes Uzziah’s own reason for leaving from the priests’ effort to hurry him out.
Presents the king’s account of an ambush as the Arameans’ established intention.
Tests their chosen chance of survival against the city option they explicitly reject.
Ranks separate battle reports by mention order without testing a meaningful distinction between them.
The key “the news” never specifies what was reported and barely tests comprehension.
Clearly tests the target of Jeroboam’s arrest order rather than confusing that target with the king.
Identifies the priests’ target, but naming Azariah among the followers largely rules out the proposed misreading.
Requires tracking whose child “my son” denotes within the woman’s quoted proposal.
Distinguishes Zechariah’s instruction from Amaziah’s example of right conduct.
Separates Elisha’s warning to the doubting officer from his earlier prediction about food prices.
Tests obedience as the reason for refusal, not the hypothetical size of a reward.
Only retrieves the last narrated action before departure, an arbitrary boundary within Paul’s activities.
Asks only which action comes first in a short list of military preparations.
Distinguishes Jehoiada, who distributes the weapons, from David, their former owner.
Tests accusers versus the council, but “the addressee” makes the stem needlessly technical.
Separates the people’s purpose of installing a king from the circumstance of Amaziah’s death.
Distinguishes the army’s commanders from the officials who muster its divisions.
Tests the crucial victim identity across shifting pronouns and two distinct prophetic figures.
Clear victim identification, but it repeats the officer-trampling target with a simpler pronoun link.
“You ... and you ... are all to guard” includes both sets of companies, not just the keyed two.
Meaningfully distinguishes the letter’s sender from its recipient using the heading alone.
Separates the Philistine killed by Abishai from David, whom Abishai rescues.
Targets the men’s meaningful change from hiding spoils to reporting the good news.
Distinguishes the young information-bearer from Paul, who arranges his access to the commander.
The report matters to the ensuing plunder, but the stem tests only immediate narrative order.
Resolves the stated motive to Uzziah rather than attributing it to his agricultural workers.
“First” misleadingly suggests both children were eaten, although the other child was hidden.
Clearly separates the person who intercedes from the king who requests and benefits from the prayer.
Distinguishes the three named enemies from the Ammonites, who bring tribute instead.
The city and tomb are nested destinations, making “first” an artificial sequence distinction.
“Ahaziah’s son’s nurse” is a cumbersome relational clue that nearly supplies the child’s identity.
Tests the stated cause of the city’s calm rather than confusing that cause with accompanying rejoicing.
Distinguishes the centurions receiving the order from the soldiers they must prepare.
Separates the imagined attacking kings from Israel’s king, whom the Arameans believe hired them.
Tests the crucial distinction between the king authorizing violence and the messenger carrying it out.
Tracks the intended guest through the old prophet’s quoted instructions without treating the claim as true.
Tests Paul’s stated reason for the long speech rather than a background detail about the room.
Distinguishes the returning soldiers from the cavalry continuing Paul’s escort.
Tests the reversal in which the would-be exorcists become victims of the possessed man.
Cured illnesses can naturally be said to leave too, so the key depends on copying the verb “left.”
Distinguishes the commander expected to bring Paul from the council petitioning for his appearance.
“Assembling materials” obscures the scrolls and turns their public renunciation into an arbitrary sequencing task.
Tests the scope of the explicit sword order, distinguishing followers from the woman being escorted out.
Distinguishes the noise prompting Athaliah’s arrival from the sight she encounters afterward.
The broad prerequisite question does not exclude Paul’s transfer as another condition before the attack.
Targets the correct recipient of the warning, but “Whose body is warned” is syntactically awkward.
Distinguishes the future Josiah’s prophesied action from Jeroboam’s present activity at the altar.
